title: Proposal: is.natural and is.whole functions to disambiguate is.count
description:
I recently discovered `assertthat `and I'm loving it. However, I ran into a little snag.

I find the name of the function `is.count` somewhat confusing. In my usage, a "count" should include the possibility that the count of x is zero, yet `is.count(x)` returns FALSE if x is zero. Perhaps I'm not thinking broadly enough, but I cannot readily think of any use case where it is impossible for a count to be zero. If such cases exist, I would expect them to be the exception rather than the rule.

Rather than quibbling on what properly or intuitively constitutes a "count", I propose the creation of two new functions that use well-defined mathematical terms to unambiguously specify the difference:

```
# TRUE if x is a natural number (positive integer, zero excluded)
is.natural <- function(x) {
  assertthat::is.count(x)
}

# TRUE if x is a whole number (non-negative integer, zero included)
is.whole <- function(x) {
  assertthat::is.count(x) || x == 0
}
```

Since `assertthat::is.count` is probably extensively used in existing packages, this proposal would not affect existing code yet it would probably help new users of `assertthat` avoid all the bugs I ran into because of my different understanding of what constitutes a "count"!

If this proposal is approved, I could write the code, test it with `testthat`, and then create a pull request.

title: Option to add a class to `assert_that` error message
description: The `rlang` package makes it possible to add classes to the error conditions (e.g. `rlang::abort`). This is a convenient feature for later working with the error messages. There are for example good for programmatically responding to errors within packages. The current option is to parse the error messages but as these can be quite dynamic to make them informative to users it would be better to have error classes. An implementation would be quite simple as the class argument should be added to the `assert_that` function and the `assertError` function. If desirable I can make a  pull request

title: is.scalar to include is.atomic?
description:
Hi,
the test for scalar evaluates also complex data types to true. For example
```
assertthat::is.scalar(list("foo"))
[1] TRUE
```
This was quite unexpected to me, because it is also documented together with the test for atomic data types.

Is there a rationale not to test for the given value to be atomic? Otherwise I would propose to test:
```
assertthat::is.scalar <- function (x) {
    is.atomic(x) && length(x) == 1L
}
```
Thanks for your help,
Manuel

description:

title: error occurs in the inner function, but only reported in the outer function
description:
When calling nested functions, the error is reported in the outer function `outer_f()`, while it happens in the inner function `inner_f()`. In complex cases this is very difficult to debug.

The correct error message (`"inner_f"`) is reported if we:
- use `stopifnot()`  instead of `assert_that()`
- do not override the `msg` argument

I suspect this has something to do with lazy evaluation, but not sure.

``` r
inner_f <- function(argument) {
  assertthat::assert_that(argument > 0, msg = "inner_f")
  argument
}

outer_f <- function(argument) {
  assertthat::assert_that(argument > 0, msg = "outer_f")
}

outer_f(inner_f(0))
#> Error: outer_f
```

title: feature proposal: suggest_that() to give warnings instead of errors
description:
**Feature proposal**: Adding a warning feature to the `assertthat` package.

**See also**: https://github.com/hadley/assertthat/issues/37

**Naming ideas**:
- `recommend_that()`
Rationale: If the recommendation is not followed, then a warning is given.
- `suggest_that()`
Rationale: If the suggestion is not followed, we warn the user. This is shorter to type and say, so seems better.

**Usage**:
- Analogous to `assert_that()`. 
  - So for example: `suggest_that(length(x) > 10)` if more than 10 elements in `x` are suggested by the function.
- If the condition is not fulfilled, then a warning is issued. 
  - In the example above for example: `Warning: length(x) not greater than 10`
- The warning message text is the same as the `assert_that()` one.
  - Consider automatically replacing "must" by "should" etc.
  - But ideally the messages would not have such verbs in them, but are just factual ("x is not abc" instead of "x must be abc")

**Implementation**:
- starting point: https://github.com/hadley/assertthat/blob/master/R/assert-that.r and https://github.com/hadley/assertthat/blob/master/R/validate-that.R  
- required functions:
  - `suggest_that()` (similar like `assert_that()`)
  - `suggestWarning()` (similar like `assertError()`)
  - `error_to_warning_msg()` (only if we want to replace verbs in the message as mentioned above)
- tests: similar like https://github.com/hadley/assertthat/blob/master/tests/testthat/test-assert-that.R 

Any feedback on this? Does it make sense? I would be happy to provide a PR :-)

title: License, and License clarity
description:
The company I work at are trying to open source some R code, but we're running into the situation that GPLv2 is incompatible with GPLv3, making it impossible for us to put an open source license our code that satisfies the requirements of both.

The only reference I see in your repository to the license is in DESCRIPTION, which currently labels it GPL-v3. Other than that, there doesn't appear to be a LICENSE file in your repository, or anything else indicating that the code is deliberately licensed under the GPLv3.

Tidyverse and r-lib have recently been aggressively re-licensing their code to be MIT [eg ggplot2's thread on the subject here: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/4232 ]. Would you be open to adjusting the license on your code to also be MIT? Or if the GPL aligns with your personal stance on open source, perhaps GPLv2-or-higher, to avoid as many incompatibilities as possible?

title: mid-pipe assertions
description:
Often when troubleshooting a "long" `%>%` pipe, if I need to test assertions on the data, I need to interrupt the pipe (if no grouping present) or use a `do()` block (both with/without grouping).

```r
library(dplyr)
cyls <- 6
mtcars %>%
  filter(cyl == cyls) %>%
  group_by(vs) %>%
  summarize(z = max(density(mpg)$y))
```

works as one might expect. If you run this with `cyls <- 4`, though, you'll see that `vs=0` only contains one row, and errors out.

```r
cyls <- 4
mtcars %>%
  filter(cyl == cyls) %>%
  group_by(vs) %>%
  mutate(z = max(density(mpg)$y))
# Error in mutate_impl(.data, dots) : 
#   need at least 2 points to select a bandwidth automatically
```

In order to assert that sufficient data is present, you either need to use a `do()` block or break up the pipe:

```r
library(assertthat)
cyls <- 4
mtcars %>%
  filter(cyl == cyls) %>%
  group_by(vs) %>%
  do({
    assert_that(
      length(na.omit(.$mpg)) > 1,
      msg = "I cannot grok the data"
    )
    .
  }) %>%
  summarize(z = max(density(mpg)$y))
# Error: I cannot grok the data
```

It would be nice to be able to test the assertion mid-pipe:

```r
cyls <- 4
mtcars %>%
  filter(cyl == cyls) %>%
  group_by(vs) %>%
  assert_pipe_stop(
    length(na.omit(mpg)) > 1,
    .msg = "I cannot grok the data"
  ) %>%
  summarize(z = max(density(mpg)$y))
```

Granted, in this contrived example, the error should be sufficient, but it's not hard to consider longer pipelines where calculation should not continue without verified conditions.

I think assertion-companion functions such as `assert_pipe_stop` and perhaps `assert_pipe_warning` might be useful. I think it makes more sense to extend `assertthat` to be pipe-aware vice adding assertions to `dplyr` or another of the `tidyverse` packages.

Thoughts?

I'm willing to work on a PR, though admittedly I'm not as proficient at NSE, where these functions would heavily reside.

title: "bad error message" redux
description:
I have [previously](https://github.com/hadley/assertthat/issues/43) reported an issue about getting "bad error message", which was [fixed](https://github.com/hadley/assertthat/pull/45), but now I have run into another instance of it. Here is some code that produces the error for me:

```R
library(assertthat)
library(fs)
# Works fine (assertion fails normally)
assert_that(all(file_exists(c("/this/path/does/not/exist/fileA", "/this/p", "C"))))
# One char longer: "bad error message"
assert_that(all(file_exists(c("/this/path/does/not/exist/fileA", "/this/pa", "C"))))

## Returns 1 element
see_if(all(file_exists(c("/this/path/does/not/exist/fileA", "/this/p", "C"))))
## One char longer: Returns 2 elements
see_if(all(file_exists(c("/this/path/does/not/exist/fileA", "/this/pa", "C"))))
```

As shown by the `see_if` calls at the bottom, the problem coincides with the vector length that causes `see_if` to return a vector of length greater than 1.

title: assert_that says "or" when it means "and" on ||-chained assertions
description:
Example:

```
> assertthat::assert_that(is.numeric("foo") || is.flag("foo"))
Error: "foo" is not a numeric or integer vector or "foo" is not a flag (a length one logical vector).
```

This is incorrect. The error is that "foo" is not numeric *and* foo is not a flag. i.e., `not(x or y) = not(x) and not(y)`. Better would be

```
Error: "foo" is not a numeric or integer vector and "foo" is not a flag (a length one logical vector).
```

AFAICS, simply replacing "or" with "and" will work. I think that would make error messages clearer. If you agree this is a bug worth fixing, I'll send a pull request.

title: 'see_if(FALSE)' generates an error
description:
The command `see_if(FALSE)` generates the following error:

    Error in get_message(res, assertion, env) : is.call(call) is not TRUE 

It seems to me this is an undesirable effect, as an error can be raised while `FALSE` is unexpected.

title: Improve combination of 'see_if()' and 'assert_that()'
description:
If I use `assert_that` and `see_if` in the same command, the message `msg` passed to `see_if` is reused by `assert_that` when necessary:

     x <- 2
    assert_that(see_if(x == 1, msg = "incorrect value"))
    #> Error: incorrect value    

However, if I desynchronize the call to `see_if` and that to `assert_that`, the message is lost: 

    test <- see_if(x == 1, msg = "incorrect value")
    assert_that(test)
    #> Error in get_message(res, assertion, env) : is.call(call) is not TRUE

It would be desirable to reuse the `see_if` message in `assert_that` in the later case, to manage cases where `see_if` is used in an `is_xxx()` like function (that tests an object) and an `assert_that(is_xxx(object))` command is used in another function.

title: Showing actual value in case of failed assertion
description:
Example:

title: feature request: has_package()
description:
This idea follows from the ["Suggests" section](http://r-pkgs.had.co.nz/description.html#dependencies) of the R-pkgs book, where you provide the code:

```R
if (!requireNamespace("pkg", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Package \"pkg\" needed for this function to work. Please install it.",
    call. = FALSE)
}
```

Could this be useful as a new assertion,`has_package()`?

```R
assertthat::has_package("dplyr")
```

I'd be happy to make the PR if you think this might be useful. If so, some questions:

1. Name: `has_package()`, `has_packages()`, other?
1. Should the argument be `...` as unnamed, or `packages` which would be a character-vector of package names, or other?

title: "bad error message" when asserting blocks and long lines of code
description:
Certain expressions cause a "bad error message" error if the assertion fails:

```R
> assert_that({FALSE})
Error in stop(assertError(attr(res, "msg"))) : bad error message
> assert_that(4 %>% sqrt %>% multiply_by(10) %>% divide_by(5) %>% add(13) %>% subtract(20) %>% equals(0)) 
Error in stop(assertError(attr(res, "msg"))) : bad error message
```

The reason is that the error message returned by `see_if` has multiple elements in it:

```R
> see_if({FALSE})
[1] FALSE
attr(,"msg")
[1] "{ is not TRUE"         "    FALSE is not TRUE" "} is not TRUE"        
> see_if(4 %>% sqrt %>% multiply_by(10) %>% divide_by(5) %>% add(13) %>% subtract(20) %>% equals(0)) 
[1] FALSE
attr(,"msg")
[1] "`%>%`(lhs = 4 %>% sqrt %>% multiply_by(10) %>% divide_by(5) %>%  is not TRUE"
[2] "    add(13) %>% subtract(20), rhs = equals(0)) is not TRUE"                  
```

Presumably somewhere a `str_c(collapse="\n")` or similar needs to be added.

title: "argument is of length zero" case uninformative
description:
Hello! I just installed your package. I noticed it does better than 'stopifnot' when comparing to a NULL:

```
> stopifnot(1==NULL) # No error
> assert_that(1==NULL)
Error in if (!res) { : argument is of length zero
```

This means that I can use it to check that e.g. `nrow(X)==N`, which is great! However, it gives even prettier errors when the argument is FALSE:

```
> assert_that(1==2)
Error: 1 not equal to 2
```

Are there any plans to, for example, have pretty errors when the argument is of length zero? For example:

```
> assert_that(1==NULL)
Error in "1==NULL" : argument is of length zero
```

This would make it a bit easier to track down the location of the error, although I guess there's always `traceback()`...

title: setting on_failure from an error handler
description:
Question (not a bug report or other similar issue):

I love the `on_failure` idea of custom messages for validation functions, but there's one (somewhat common, I think) scenario that I've had difficulty implementing without resorting to a sort of 'hack'.

In the (documentation example, `is_odd` has the first embedded `assert_that` testing for a numeric scalar `x`.
What if we wanted `is_odd` to _always_ return `TRUE` or `FALSE`, and instead push the error message pertaining the `x`'s bad type to the wrapping (outer) `assert_that`?

Here's a more concrete example, where the function `string_is_foobar` should always return `TRUE` or `FALSE` on its own, but when wrapped in an `assert_that` call generate the 'correct' error message:

``` R
string_is_foobar <- function(x) {
    tryCatch({
        assert_that(is.string(x))
        assert_that(are_equal(x, "foobar"))
        return(TRUE)
    }, error = function(e) {
        ## this next assignment seems dangerous/kludgey, and might fail due to namespace issues
        on_failure(string_is_foobar) <<- function(call, env) conditionMessage(e)
        return(FALSE)
    })
}
```

And here's the behavior (which also happens to be the desired behavior):

``` R
> string_is_foobar("foobar")
[1] TRUE
> string_is_foobar("foobaz")
[1] FALSE
> string_is_foobar(10)
[1] FALSE
> assert_that(string_is_foobar("foobar"))
[1] TRUE
> assert_that(string_is_foobar("foobaz"))
Error: x not equal to "foobar"
> assert_that(string_is_foobar(10))
Error: x is not a string (a length one character vector).
```

The `tryCatch` helps enforce the fail-fast behavior within `string_is_foobar` without using a long list of conditionals.
But my hack where I assign the `on_failure` behavior within the `tryCatch` `error` handler seems a but kludgey/dangerous, as it relies on finding `string_is_foobar` by name.
I tried to use `parent.frame` and `sys.function` from within the `error` function in order to gain a reference back to the executed `string_is_foobar` function, but to no avail.

So, I'm wondering if there's actually a better paradigm for this in general.
Desires:
- Start with a testing function that returns `TRUE` or `FALSE` in (nearly) all conditions, with the expectation that to truly 'fail', it must be wrapped in an assertion.
- Have this testing function also possess fail-fast behavior, such that any internal `assert_that` failure ends execution of the function (and thus causes the function to return `FALSE`).
- Have the 'appropriate' error message displayed when the testing function itself is wrapped in an `assert_that`, where 'appropriate' means the message corresponds to the specific failing case within the testing function.

Any ideas?

Cheers, and thanks much for all the work!

title: match.arg-like assertion
description:
The general R practice to supply non-binary, enum-like options to functions is

```
myfun <- function(option=c("foo", "bar", "foobar") {
  option <- match.arg(option)
  ...
}
```

So how about an assertion that supports this? Just because then I can handle all arguments the same way, in a single `assert_that` call. E.g.

```
  assert_that(is.enum(option))
```

Personally I like partial matching and if this is case-insensitive, so maybe it could be `is.enum(option, ignore_case=TRUE, partial_match=TRUE)`.

The only glitch is that I will need to write `option <- (my)match.arg(option)` anyway, after the check, and this checks `option`, too. But there is not much to do about this, probably.

title: Access default argument values in custom assertion error messages
description:
It would be very useful if it was possible to access default argument values in custom assertion error messages, but I don't think this is possible at the moment, as we only have available the data from `match.call` (see also here: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/14397364/match-call-with-default-arguments).

For example, I think it could be useful if code like the following worked as expected:

```
# check a vector contains only values 33 or 64
valid_phred <- function(phred, options=c(33, 64)) {
    assert_that(is.numeric(phred))
    all(phred %in% c(33, 64))
}

# custom error message - would be nice if we didn't have to hard code "33 and 64" 
on_failure(valid_phred) <- function(call, env) {
    paste("Invalid phred score - must be one of:", paste(call$options, collapse=", "))
}

assert_that(valid_phred(c(33, 64, 32)))
# Error: Invalid phred score - must be one of: 33, 64
```

title: proper use of on_failure and assertthat documentation?
description:
Hi Hadley,

I didn't know if it'd be better to pose a directed question here or on SO since there aren't any good tags for this package, and all assertthat queries return info from other languages - let me know if I should move this over there.

I'm trying to understand 'proper' documentation of on_failure, here is the code I have:

```
is_ObsName <- function(x, obs_names) {
  x %in% obs_names
}

on_failure(is_ObsName) <- function(call, env = parent.env) {
#do stuff
}
```

Where `ObsName` is the argument passed into the function and `obs_names` is a vector of unique observation names extracted from a df.

Currently, if I just `import` assertthat my package won't build properly and gives the error:

```
Error in on_failure(is_ObsName) <- function(call, env = parent.env) { : 
  could not find function "on_failure<-"
```

If I change assertthat to `depends` so asserthat is loaded the package builds and works properly.

description: Otherwise, the type of the return value depends on the result of the evaluation. It's a potentially breaking change, though.

title: Custom information message on error
description:
The automatic construction of failure messages is handy, but does not help when building assertions that are to return a user-friendly text for a complex condition. (Example: Checking that a directory does not contain files with certain names, printing the offending names on error. I could craft a function to test it, and another one to pass to `on_failure`, but this is just a one-time check -- too much work.)

I see that `get_message` checks the result for a `"msg"` attribute, with early return, so the following works (=fails) as expected:

```
assert_that(structure(FALSE, msg="Custom message"))
```

But this is not documented, so I think we're not supposed to use it...

@hadley: Would you review a patch that adds a `msg` parameter to `assert_that`?

title: assert_that(all(FALSE)) stops with unrelated error message
description:
```
> assert_that(all(FALSE))
Error in !res : invalid argument type
```

Workaround:

```
> assert_that(!!all(FALSE))
Error: !(!all(FALSE)) is not TRUE
```

Also, I would have expected that `assert_that` also accepts a vector of booleans -- after all, it is advertised as a drop-in replacement for `stopifnot`:

```
> assert_that(c(TRUE, FALSE))
Error: assert_that: assertion has length greater than 1
```
